text: Imagine renting an AI data center full of flagship GPUs, chips capable of nearly one quadrillion floating-point operations every second.
Now open your profiler while users chat with your model.
In the decode phase, the Tensor Cores may be nowhere near full utilization.
The memory system can be working flat out while much of the GPU’s peak computing capacity goes unused.
And when engineers grouped 32 requests together, classic request-level batching created a new problem: it was like forcing Usain Bolt to jog beside one slow essay writer while 31 fast readers waited.
How does a massively parallel chip end up waiting for data, and how did a Tetris-style scheduler help serving systems process far more requests?
To understand the stall, look at the two phases of an LLM chat turn: prefill and decode.
During prefill, the model processes prompt tokens together through large matrix operations.
If you send a prompt containing 1,000 tokens, each model weight can contribute to the computation for many token positions in the same pass.
That lets the GPU reuse weight data across a large amount of math.
Take an NVIDIA H100 SXM as an example.
Its dense BF16 Tensor Core peak is about 989 trillion floating-point operations per second, and its HBM bandwidth is about 3.35 trillion bytes per second.
Divide compute by bandwidth and you get a roofline ridge point of roughly 295 floating-point operations per byte.
In a simplified weight-only example, a 1,000-token prefill can reuse each two-byte BF16 weight across many token positions, producing arithmetic intensity high enough to become compute-bound.
Then decode begins, and the balance changes.
Each new token depends on the previous one, so one chat stream generates its next token sequentially.
For a large model whose weights do not fit in on-chip cache, the model must read its weights again for that step, while producing just one new token.
With two bytes per BF16 weight and roughly two floating-point operations per multiply-add, that is about one operation per byte of weight traffic.
That is far below the H100’s roughly 295-FLOPs-per-byte ridge.
Batching helps because one weight read can serve several users at once.
In the same simplified model, 32 requests sharing a weight read reach about 32 operations per byte, still well below the ridge.
The result is not that the entire GPU is idle.
The memory system may be saturated while the Tensor Cores remain underused.
Real performance also depends on model size, precision, context length, and KV-cache traffic.
So the obvious fix is to batch more users.
Once the GPU has loaded model weights for a decode step, applying them to more active token vectors can add substantial computation without proportionally increasing weight traffic.
But classic request-level batching creates a different bottleneck.
Picture 32 requests entering one static batch.
Requests one through 31 ask quick questions: "Yes or no?" "Fix this one-line bug." They finish in 15 tokens.
Request 32 asks for a 2,000-token architecture essay.
In a fixed request-level batch, the scheduler cannot simply replace the finished requests with new arrivals.
The group remains tied to its slowest member.
For the remaining 1,985 token steps, the batch has one active request instead of 32.
Depending on the implementation, finished positions may also cause padding or other unnecessary work.
Their reserved KV-cache memory can remain tied up as well.
Meanwhile, new users wait in the queue because those batch positions cannot be reused until the group completes.
That is head-of-line blocking.
The key question is simple: why schedule whole requests when the GPU executes inference one iteration at a time?
The Orca paper, published in 2022, introduced iteration-level scheduling.
Today, this general approach is widely known as continuous batching.
Instead of waiting for all 32 requests to finish together, the scheduler rebuilds the batch after each generation step.
The instant a request emits its end-of-sequence token, it leaves the active batch.
A waiting request can take its place in the next iteration.
The batch stays populated as requests finish and new ones arrive.
It sounds straightforward, until those requests have very different sequence lengths.
